pr_title: Remove fragile NGen logic for precomputed hashcodes
pr_comments: Have you done any measurements to see whether it would be worth it to cache the hashcodes at runtime?

> Have you done any measurements to see whether it would be worth it to cache the hashcodes at runtime?

I didn't. I interpreted your statement on the issue as the effort wasn't worth it. I will go back and determine any actual benefit/cost.

@jkotas and @EgorBo 

I ran the numbers for implementing the hash or just performing the string compare. The hash was computed lazily during the loop [here](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/ffbcb8336ac67496b0565112f663f74fda6cac34/src/coreclr/vm/memberload.cpp#L1118-L1143). The below numbers are from a Windows x64 machine using QPC for the time in the loop. The data below is in QPC units. These numbers are very small except in cases when we need to compute the hash. The overall time spent is higher due to the hash and I'm not sure adding the noise for the hash compute is a good idea given how small the win is in practice.

I could see an argument for the work if there was a place where we could precompute the hash but even then it isn't clear the win would be a real win.

Your thoughts?

```
hash
N: 39_656
sum: 587_307
stddev:747.932828
mean:14.81004136

no hash
N: 39_672
sum: 455_516
stddev:29.93566039
mean:11.48205283
```
I'm going to put up a change removing all the logic given I don't see a lot of value in adding back this hashing.

> I'm going to put up a change removing all the logic given I don't see a lot of value in adding back this hashing.

Sounds good. Thank you for collecting the numbers.

> The hash was computed lazily during the loop [here](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/ffbcb8336ac67496b0565112f663f74fda6cac34/src/coreclr/vm/memberload.cpp#L1118-L1143).

For reference, could you please share commit with the code that was used to compute the hash lazily?

> > The hash was computed lazily during the loop [here](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/ffbcb8336ac67496b0565112f663f74fda6cac34/src/coreclr/vm/memberload.cpp#L1118-L1143).
> 
> For reference, could you please share commit with the code that was used to compute the hash lazily?

Yep. I am going to push up the reverted commit.
@jkotas CI is green. The commit with perf collection logic is at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/82563/commits/8d45974a0166e2e51a469d532d4801cf9bdb7ae3.

> https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/82563/commits/8d45974a0166e2e51a469d532d4801cf9bdb7ae3#diff-3d5bc2c8419db164831e65cf277753ec74887f9298025abcf75119781a5cea0aR1152-R1154

This is very expensive way to compute the hashcode. It converts the UTF8 string to UTF16 string first and then computes the hashcode of the UTF16 string. We do not need the case-insensitive hashcodes for the type loader purposes. All name matching in the type loader is case sensitive. A simple case-sensitive hashcode like `HashStringA` would be enough. I expect that the numbers would be a lot better with a simple case-sensitive hashcode like `HashStringA`, I am not sure by how much.

@jkotas Using `HashStringA` is negligibly faster.

```
hash - using HashStringA
N: 39_663
sum: 553_067
stddev:777.0471155
mean:13.9441545
```

> It converts the UTF8 string to UTF16 string first and then computes the hashcode of the UTF16 string. 

I don't think that is true in this case. The `ConvertToIteratable();` call checks if the string can be [coerced to ASCII first](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/49553e8a9e89d9d209095eed848f7bcae848ac4b/src/coreclr/inc/sstring.inl#L1879-L1881). Since we are only using ASCII for SPCL and our libs it just marks the representation as such and performs the same sort of hash.

issue_context.title: enum_packedSlotLayout_NameHashMask is unused
issue_context.body:
I noticed that `MemberLoader::FindMethod` shows up in traces, namely [strcmp](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/463954dbc728470fb21a097188fc3dae91f6cbe4/src/coreclr/vm/memberload.cpp#L1135) inside it 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/523221/220316519-8fee6dd7-1ac3-4d1a-9b27-c52ead6cc5fc.png)

It seems that logic in `FindMethod` implies MethodDesc might store a hash for method name inside `m_wSlotNumber` for faster name comparison but aparently it's never used since `enum_packedSlotLayout_NameHashMask` is never set. see [MethodDesc::MightHaveName](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/463954dbc728470fb21a097188fc3dae91f6cbe4/src/coreclr/vm/method.cpp#L387-L409)

Same for fields' names.

PS: I'm profiling first 2 seconds of Paint.NET start

cc @jkotas
comments:
cc @AaronRobinsonMSFT 

The hashcode fast-path was an optimization done by fragile NGen that precomputed and stored the hashcodes at build-time.

It is not obvious whether this optimization is worth it when the hashcodes are computed at runtime: We would spend time computing and storing the hashcodes, hoping that these lookups happen often enough to offset the cost.

review_comments: This is the only use of HashCaseInsensitive method. It can be deleted.
